Menstrual function disorders: assessment and investigation #5

  • the most common presentation of female gonadal disease
  • Definitions
  • • Primary amenorrhea=failure of menarche by the age of 15-16 years.
  • • Secondary amenorrhea=the cessation of menses for >6 months in ♀ who had previously menstruated or no menses for more than three cycles in an individual who has previously had cyclic menses.
  • • Oligomenorrhoea is defined as the reduction in the frequency of menses to <9 periods a year.

Ovarian insufficiency or ♀ hypogonadism #6

  • Definition:
  • ovarian insufficiency also termed hypogonadism is defined as diminished functional activity of the ovaries—that may result in diminished production of sex hormones (estrogen deficiency)

Classification of ♀ hypogonadism (ovarian insufficiency) #7

  • According to the site of the lesion:
  • o Secondary /central hypogonadism (this is usually caused by diseases of the pituitary gland or hypothalamus), also referred to as hypogonadotropic hypogonadism
  • o Primary /peripheral hypogonadism (means that the ovaries do not function normally), also known as ovarian failure
  • (!!!it may occur at any time from embryonic development onward; if it occurs in ♀ prior to age 40, it is called premature ovarian failure or insufficiency (POF/POI)).
  • According to the age at onset:
  • o before puberty
  • o after puberty

Slide 8 #8

Table. Classification of amenorrhea and ovarian insufficiency
Primary Amenorrhea + Absent breast development (or ♀ hypogonadism with prepubertal onset)
Primary ovarian insufficiency Gonadal agenesis Gonadal dysgenesis (45 XO: Turner syndrome and its variants: mosaicism (e.g., X/XX, X/XX/XXX)) 46,XX or 46,XY (Swyer syndrome) pure gonadal dysgenesis Defects in estrogen biosynthesis (e.g., CYP17 α-deficiency)
Secondary ovarian insufficiency (see also chapter pituitary insufficiency) Inadequate GnRH synthesis (Kallmann syndrome) Developmental anatomic abnormalities in central nervous system Constitutional delay in puberty CNS neoplasm (craniopharyngioma, gliomas), pituitary tumors Isolated gonadotropin insufficiency Combined pituitary insufficiency Prepubertal hypothyroidism

Slide 9 #9

Table. Classification of amenorrhea and ovarian insufficiency
Amenorrhea + Breast development (or ♀ hypogonadism with postpubertal onset)
Primary ovarian insufficiency POF Iatrogenic (radiation, chemotherapy) Mosaicism (eg mosaic Turner syndrome (46,XX/XO)) Infections (e.g., mumps)) Autoimmune destruction Fragile X syndrome (Fragile X premutations) (an association has been described between a distal mutation on the long arm of the X chromosome- in the FMR1 gene (fragile X gene)- the FMR1 permutation state and premature ovarian failure)
Secondary ovarian insufficiency Hypothalamic etiology Functional hypothalamic amenorrhea [a reduced GnRH drive (decrease in pulse frequency and amplitude)→↓LH, FSH →anovulation] Stress Amenorrhea associated with eating disorders (anorexia nervosa, bulimia) Amenorrhea associated with strenuous exercise-e.g., female athletes, competitors in events such as gymnastics, ballet, marathon running Chronic disease CNS neoplasm Pituitary etiology Hyperprolactinemia, pituitary tumors Acquired pituitary insufficiency (see also chapter pituitary failure)

Slide 10 #10

  • The majority of cases of secondary amenorrhea can be accounted for by four conditions:
  • • Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS).
  • • Hypothalamic amenorrhea (↓E2)
  • • Hyperprolactinemia. (↓E2)
  • • Ovarian insufficiency. (↓E2)
  • !!! PCOS is the only common endocrine cause of amenorrhea with normal estrogenization; all other causes are estrogen-deficient.
  • The causes of amenorrhea are grouped according to the level of involvement in the regulatory system that governs normal menstrual activity i.e.,
  • hypothalamic,
  • pituitary,
  • ovarian and
  • uterine.

Clinical features in ♀ hypogonadism: #11

  • OI WITH PREPUBERTAL ONSET →poor sexual secondary sexual development and eunuchoid skeletal proportions
  • 1. SEXUAL INFANTILISM
  • Primary amenorrhea
  • Absence/sparse of pubic and axillary hair
  • Absence of breast development (thelarche)
  • Infantile aspect of external and internal genitalia
  • 2.SOMATIC MODIFICATIONS
  • Tall stature, eunuchoid skeletal proportions (crown to pubis to pubis to floor ratio<1)
  • Low peak bone mass
  • 3. PSYCHOLOGICAL DISTURBANCES
  • ↓ libido

Clinical features in ♀ hypogonadism #12

  • OI WITH POSTPUBERTAL ONSET
  • Secondary amenorrhea
  • infertility
  • Decrease in axillary and pubic hair
  • Atrophy of breast
  • Involution of genital tract, urogenital atrophy →vaginal dryness and pain with intercourse, atrophic cystitis
  • Precocious appearance of wrinkles
  • Vasomotor symptoms (hot flushes)
  • Late complications: osteoporosis, atherosclerosis with↑ risk of cardiovascular and cerebrovascular disease

Workup of ♀ hypogonadism #13

Work up of primary amenorrhea with absence of sexual maturation (and no hirsutism or virilization)- ovarian insufficiency with prepubertal onset #14

  • Firstly, rule out thyroid dysfunction and hyperprolactinemia (check: TSH, FT4, and PRL)
  • TSH, free T4, PRL=normal 
  • Uterus (pelvic US/MRI) usually present
  • 2. Is it primary or secondary ovarian dysfunction/insufficiency?
  • Measure: FSH, LH, E2
  • → ↓/ low-normal FSH, LH + ↓E2 = secondary (central) ovarian insufficiency/ hypogonadotropic hypogonadism with prepubertal onset
  • In these patients, LH and FSH responses to testing with GnRH may help to differentiate delayed puberty from a more serious problem
  •  do hormonal, neuroradiologic and neuro-ophatalmologic assessment of hypothalamus and pituitary ( e.g. tumors: craniopharyngiomas)
  • → ↑ FSH, LH + ↓ E2 = primary ovarian insufficiency/hypergonadotropic hypogonadism
  • If the patient is short in stature and has obvious stigmas of Turner’s sdr → Barr test, Karyotype (45,X0)
  • If the patient is of normal height or has relatively longer arms and legs compared with the length of the trunk( eunuchoid proportions) → search for other causes of primary ovarian failure:
  • autoimmune: do anti ovary autoantibodies),
  • exclude gonadal agenesis: do sonography, laparoscopy with biopsy).

Workup of secondary amenorrhea or oligomenorrhea in the presence of normal sexual secondary characteristics, and after menarche (ovarian failure with postpubertal onset). #15

  • 1.! The possibility of pregnancy should always be considered ( pregnancy test!)
  • 2.  Measure : TSH+ FT4 to test for thyroid disease, PRL to test for hyperPRL
  • → if PRL, TSH+FT4=normal →
  • → localize the underlying cause of amenorrhea: either disruption in the HPO axis or dysfunction of the outflow tract
  • 3. Assessment of estrogen status
  • A. Indirectly (progesterone withdrawal test)
  •  by attempting to induce withdrawal uterine bleeding by adm. progesterone: eg dydrogesterone 10-20mg/day daily for 5-10 days
  • →If a bleed occurs within about 1 week after the last pill ('withdrawal bleeding'), then there is adequate estrogen priming and endometrial development (positive test)
  • If no signs of hyperandrogenism are present, then, the ♀ patient does not have a serious problem-just reassurance

Slide 16 #16

  • Negative test = failure to induce menstrual bleeding by exogenous progestin indicates:
  • → either hypoestrogenism or an outflow tract disorder.
  • 4. Do gonadotropin level: FSH, LH, + E2 to directly assess the endogenous estrogen status and to differentiate them:
  • !!! NB If there has been a recent menstrual cycle, a test on days 2 to 4 (for FSH, E2, LH) would be appropriate, but in prolonged amenorrhea, the testing can be performed on a random day.
  • ↓/ low-normal FSH, LH + ↓ E2 = Insufficient estrogen production secondary to hypothalamic-pituitary disorder
  • ↑ FSH, LH + ↓E2 = Insufficient estrogen production secondary to primary ovarian failure
  • ! A normal response ( with bleeding) following treatment with a combination of estrogen +progestin (see next) is obtained- because the outflow tract is intact
  • Normal FSH, LH, E2= ? Defect of outflow tract

Defect of the outflow tract with normal estrogen production #17

  • 5. If one suspects this, its integrity can be assessed by administering an oral combination of estrogen+ progesterone (E2 for 21-35 days adding a progestin in the last5-10 days)
  • a lack of withdrawal bleeding following treatment usually indicates an abnormality of the outflow tract
  • eg : Asherman’ s sdr← destruction of the endometrial cavity by chronic infections such as tuberculosis or destruction of the endometrium by curettage ; or
  • Mullerian defects( Mayer-Rokitansky-Kuster-Hauser sdr= a congenital condition, characterized by normal ovarian development, normal endocrine function, and normal female sexual development, but a shortened or absent vagina in addition to absence of the uterus (or varying degrees of uterine development) ( !!! Primary amenorrhea)
  • 6. Signs of hyperandrogenism (hirsutism, acne)? → evaluate for PCOS, late-onset CAH, Cushing
  • serum total T, DHEAS and 17-OHP should be measured
  • = positive progestin withdrawal test →withdrawal bleeding (PCOS women are typically well estrogenized)

Management of amenorrhea and of OI #18

  • Treatment of ovarian insufficiency with prepubertal onset
  • Sex hormone replacement therapy (HRT)
  • • Exogenous estrogens are required to compensate estrogen deficiency
  • The goals of HRT in young adolescents:
  • to develop and maintain secondary sexual characteristics, mainly breast development and feminization,
  • to induce growth spurt, to induce bone mass aquisition and to maintain bone mass.
  • Estrogens can be administered as 17β-E2, 17β-estradiol valerate (EV), conjugated estrogens, or ethinyl estradiol (EE).
  • In Europe, E2 is available in the form of a pill, transdermal (TD) patches and gel.
  • 17β-estradiol +transdermal route (or oral route) of estrogen delivery = preferred for puberty induction or to sustain puberty in girls
  • Examples:
  • e.g Vivelle Dot®, Estraderm® TD patch - doses available: 25, 37.5, 50, 75, 100 μg
  • e.g Cetura® 0.5 mg (E2 tablet)
  • -an incremental increase in the dose is recommended over a period of 2–3 years until satisfactory physical effect, usually an adult dose, has been reached

INITIAL: part of patch twice weekly; in daily practice, we cut the patches #19

  • TD: Starting dose of puberty: 3-7µg /day (part of patch twice weekly) →adult dose:25–100 μg/day
  • A progesterone is added after puberty induction or during sex HRT to sustain puberty in girls after breakthrough bleeding/ after at least 2 years of treatment
  • - a 10-day treatment given cyclically is preferred
  • -oral, natural micronised progesterone (100–200 mg daily), oral dydrogesterone (10 mg daily)
  • LATER
  • → change pubertal induction treatment of estrogen and progesterone to permanent adult sex HRT (at the end of pubertal induction) (TD or oral E2 should be the first choice )
  • OR
  • → the patient may be switched to oral contraceptives (in particular-if is for birth control,…) which are more convenient and preferred by most adolescents, although TD 17β-E2 with oral progesterone probably represents the most physiological route for HRT .
  • When the diagnosis of hypogonadism is made in childhood, the optimal age at which to start is around the age of 11 -12.
  • → up to the age of physiological menopause (≈ 50-51 years)
  • If there is a coexisting GH deficiency (in the context of pituitary failure) first treat de GH deficiency, then add estrogen replacement therapy

Slide 20 #20

  • Treatment of ovarian insufficiency with postpubertal onset – hormone replacement therapy (HRT) (estrogens and progesterone) is essential in premenopausal women.
  • The goals of HRT: to maintain secondary sex characteristics (e.g., vulvar and vaginal lubrication),
  • to prevent osteoporosis,
  • to abolish vasomotor symptoms with an improvement in sense of well-being.
  • Furthermore, HRT protects against cardiovascular risk.
  • Estrogen-progestogen regimens can be continuous (i.e., estrogen-progestogen taken every day) or follow a cyclic regimen, with estrogen taken every day and progestogen taken for 12–14 days every month.
  • e.g. CYCLO-PROGYNOVA® ( 21 tb)
  • 21 tb: Estradiol valerat 2 mg (11 tb) and estradiol valerat 2 mg + norgestrel 0,5 mg (10 tb)
  • FEMOSTON ®2/10 or 1/10 ( 28 tb)
  • 28 tb: estradiole ( 2 mg/1 mg) 14 tb + estradiole ( 2mg/1mg and didrogesterone) 14 tb
  • In adolescents or women with hysterectomy, estrogen alone can be taken every day
  • topical ( for use on skin): patch, gel/ orally
  • GnRH or FSH+ LH stimulation treatment if fertility is desired (in secondary (central) ovarian failure)

MENOPAUSE Definition: The menopause is the permanent cessation of menstruation as a result of ovarian failure and is a retrospective diagnosis made after 12 months of amenorrhea amenorrhea Morphological and structural changes in the body(←resulting mainly from the loss of estrogen production) Progressive decline in ovarian function →over a period of 15 years The menopausal transition ends with the final menstrual period, which cannot be recognized until after 12 months of amenorrhea. Mean age of menopause= 50-51 years ( 46-55 years). Early menopause or premature ovarian failure = prior <40 years(1%) When a woman's FSH blood level is consistently elevated to 40 mIU/mL or higher (e.g., FSH >40 UI/l on two different occasions ), and she has not had a menstrual period for a year, it is generally accepted that she has reached menopause. #21

Hirsutism #22

  • Hirsutism=is excessive terminal hair (thick or dark hair) that appears in a male pattern (excessive hair in androgen-dependent areas; i.e., sexual hair, mustache, beard, central chest, shoulders, lower abdomen, back, inner thigh) in ♀ as a result of ↑androgen production and ↑ skin sensitivity to androgens.
  • It may be accompanied by other evidence of androgen excess, such as acne, oily skin and hair, and male pattern alopecia.
  • Hypertrichosis is a separate condition. It is distributed in a generalized, nonsexual pattern (i.e., predominantly on forearms or lower legs); it may be hereditary or result from certain medications (e.g., phenytoin, cyclosporine).
Table Causes of hirsutism
PCOS 95% Androgen-secreting tumors (ovarian or adrenal) Adrenal congenital hyperplasia Cushing’s syndrome Acromegaly Severe insulin resistance Hypothyroidism Idiopathic (normal US and endocrine profile) Drugs: some progestins used in OC preparations may be androgenic (e.g., norethisterone).

Polycystic ovary syndrome #23

  • The majority of hirsutism is due to androgen excess (> 80%), and the majority of women with hirsutism (70% to 80%) have PCOS.
  • the most common endocrinopathy of women of reproductive age
  • -complex endocrine condition, due to its heterogeneity and uncertainty about its aetiology.
  • = is defined by a combination of signs and symptoms of androgen excess and ovarian dysfunction in the absence of other specific diagnoses.
  • -debates on the definition of PCOS (1990 NIH, 2003 Rotterdam criteria (updated by the ESHRE in 2018), 2006 AE-PCOS)
  • 2018 Rotterdam PCOS Diagnostic Criteria in ADULTS (two of oligo- or anovulation, clinical and/or biochemical hyperandrogenism, or polycystic ovaries on ultrasound), after exclusion of related disorders. (see the table „Causes of hirsutism”)
  • Where both oligo- or anovulation and hyperandrogenism are present, ultrasound is not necessary for diagnosis.
  • !!! In ADOLESCENTES, both oligo-anovulation and hyperandrogenism are required, with ultrasound not recommended for diagnosis.

Slide 24 #24

  • Features: oligo-/amenorrhoea (70%) due to anovulation, hirsutism, seborrhea, and/or acne, and androgenic alopecia or male pattern balding, insulin resistance, overweight/obesity, ± infertility.
  • Standardized visual scales are preferred when assessing hirsutism, such as the modified Ferriman Gallwey score (mFG) with a level ≥ 4-6 indicating hirsutism, depending on ethnicity
  • Laboratory
  • Testosterone (T)/ calculated bioavailable T/ Free androgen index: FAI = 100 x (total T/SHBG) may be ↑, SHBG ↓ (owing to the hyperinsulinaemic state), DHEAS, androstendione - may be ↑
  • To rule out other disorders: prolactin, TSH, FT4, 17-OH-progesterone (late-onset CAH)
  • Treatment
  • Treatment should be symptom-oriented, long term and dynamic and adapted to the changing circumstances, personal needs and expectations of the individual patient.
  • Therapeutic approaches should target hyperandrogenism, the consequences of ovarian dysfunction and/or the associated metabolic disorders.
  • Combined oral contraceptive pill (COCP) →useful for amenorrhoea and hirsutism
  • For hirsutism:
  • Androgen receptor blockers: Spironolactone 100-200 mg/day (+COCP)
  • mechanical methods of hair removal, such as electrolysis and laser therapy.
  • Metformin – obese women and those with insulin resistance
  • Weight loss

Turner sdr ( syndrome of gonadal dysgenesis) #25

  • Most common X chromosome abnormality in ♀, affecting 1:2,500 live ♀ births.
  • Result of complete or partial absence of an X chromosome.
  • The classical form= 45, X0 karyotype represents 50% of all patients with X Cs abnormalities
  • Structural rearrangement of the X chromosome, and/or Mosaicism : 45X0/46XX, 45X0/46XX/47XXX
  • Clinical presentation: the cardinal features of 45, X0 gonadal dysgenesis are a variety of somatic anomalies, sexual infantilism at puberty secondary to gonadal dysgenesia and short stature
  • I. Somatic anomalies
  • In infancy: lymphedema of the extremities
  • Later in life: typical facies : micrognathia, a fish-like mouth with a narrow, high- arched palate, hypertelorism, epicanthus, ptosis, strabismus, prominent, low-set, ears
  • short, thick and webbed neck; low posterior hairline
  • broad chest with widely spaced inverted nipples, multiple pigmented nevi, cubitus valgus (Madelung deformity of the wrist), short 4th metacarpals
  • There is an increased risk of celiac disease, autoimmune thyroiditis, diabetes mellitus, rheumatoid arthritis, inflammatory bowel disease, recurrent otitis media
  • cardiovascular defects-especially coarctation of aorta and nonstenotic bicuspid aorta- and kidney anomalies: horseshoe kidney, duplication of the renal pelvis and ureter

Slide 26 #26

  • typical facies : micrognathia, a fish-like mouth with a narrow, high- arched palate, hypertelorism, epicanthus, ptosis, strabismus, prominent, low-set, ears
  • short, thick and webbed neck; low posterior hairline
  • broad chest with widely spaced inverted nipples,

Turner sdr ( syndrome of gonadal dysgeneis) #27

  • II. Short stature
  • Is an invariable feature of the syndrome; mean final height in 45, X0 patients is 143cm (mean:133-153 cm)
  • ← ! Is not due to a deficiency of GH, IGF-I, sex steroids, or thyroid hormone
  • ← [it is related, at least in part, to haploinsufficiency of the PHOG (pseudoautosomal homeobox osteogenic gene)/SHOX (short stature homeobox gene) in the pseudoautosomal region of the X ]
  • III. Gonadal dysgenesis
  • The gonads : ovarian follicles undergo premature apoptosis resulting in fibrous streaks as typical histologic finding.
  • The genital tract and external genitalia are female in character but immature
  • Because ovarian function is impaired, puberty does not usually ensue spontaneously and hence, primary amenorrhea and sexual infantilism are hallmarks of this syndrome.

Laboratory findings #28

  • Hormonal evaluation
  • FSH, LH↑ + ↓E2
  • Diagnosis
  • Barr test ( determination of the X chromatin pattern (Barr body)- negative
  • Karyotype analysis is the definitive procedure: 45,X0 / mosaicism

Laboratory findings #29

  • X-ray findings: shortening of the fourth metacarpal, scoliosis
  •  Bone densitometry (DXA): osteoporosis
  • All patients with Turner syndrome should have a complete cardiac evaluation by a cardiologist at diagnosis as well as periodic follow-up echocardiography or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) as necessary to monitor aortic diameter and cardiovascular status.
  • Routine intravenous urography or renal sonography is also indicated to detect a surgically correctable renal abnormality.
  • Ultrasonography of the pelvis or MRI: rudimentary ovaries/streak gonads, small uterus

Treatment of Turner sdr #30

  • Objectives→ directed toward
  • maximizing final height and
  • inducing secondary sexual characteristics and menarcha at an age commensurate with that of normal peers
  • Although the short stature is not due ←↓GH, administration of high-dose biosynthetic human GH results in an increase in final height
  • → give recombinant GH 45-50µg/kg/day
  • → in patients who have been treated with GH and have achieved an acceptable height, estrogen replacement therapy (17 ꞵ E2) should start between 11 and 12 years of age with low dose, increasing to adult dosing over 2–3 years ;
  • ( use transdermal 17 Beta estradiol (=preferred), if available)
  • … adding progesterone once breakthrough bleeding occurs, or after 2 years of estrogen treatment

MALE HYPOGONADISM (MH) #31

  • Definition: Failure of testes to produce adequate amounts of testosterone, spermatozoa, or both.
  • MH CLASSIFICATION
  • According to the site of the lesion:
  •  Secondary/central male hypogonadism ← as a result of hypothalamic or pituitary dysfunction.
  •  Primary male hypogonadism ←due to testicular failure with normal hypothalamus and pituitary function.
  • According to the age at onset:
  •  Male hypogonadism with prepubertal onset
  •  Male hypogonadism with postpubertal onset
  • Hypogonadism may be subdivided into three general categories .

Etiopathogenesis of MH #32

  • PRIMARY MH
  • Bilateral anorchia (vanishing testes sdr)
  • Noonan sdr
  • Klinefelter’s sdr
  • Iatrogenic MH: trauma, radiation
  • Orchitis
  • 25% of ♂ who develop mumps after puberty have associated orchitis, and 25–50% of these will develop testicular failure.
  • Primary testicular failure may occur as part of an autoimmune disease.
  • Cryptorchidism
  • 75% of ♂ with bilateral cryptorchidism are infertile; ↓testosterone and ↑ gonadotrophins in bilateral cryptorchidism
  • Defects in androgen biosynthesis (deficit of 17 α hydroxylase, 3β HSD deficiency)
  • CENTRAL MH (hypothalamic-pituitary disorders)
  • Panhypopituitarism
  • Isolated LH and FSH deficiency
  • Congenital
  • With hyposmia or anosmia (Kallmann syndrome)
  • Hypogonadotrophic hypogonadism (HH) ± anosmia. Results from disordered migration of GnRH-producing neurons into the hypothalamus.
  • With complex neurologic syndromes
  • Prader-Willi syndrome
  • Acquired
  • Hyperprolactinemia
  • Tumor (craniopharyngioma, pituitary adenoma, parasellar tumor)
  • Cushing syndrome
  • Iron overload (Haemochromatosis)
  • Head trauma
  • Radiotherapy, surgery to the pituitary gland or hypothalamus

Slide 33 #33

  • Complete androgen insensitivity syndrome (resistance to T due to defect in androgen receptor) caractherized by:
  • 46,XY karyotype,
  • Normal female phenotype but with inguinal hernias or labial masses, a shortened vagina, sparse axillary and pubic hair,
  • Serum T either within or above the normal range for men and boys and LH concentrations inappropriately ↑
  • Serum estradiol concentrations higher than those noted in men and boys but lower than those reported in normal women
  • Defects in androgen action ( complete androgen insensitivity-testicular feminization)
  • ← a resistance to the actions of the androgen hormones

Clinical presentation #34

  • Prenatal androgen deficiency
  •  Androgen deficiency during the second to third months of fetal development results in varying degrees of ambiguity of the genitalia and male pseudo-hermaphroditism.
  •  If the deficiency develops during the third trimester, cryptorchidism as well as micropenis may occur.
  • Prepubertal androgen deficiency (postnatal prepubertal androgen deficiency) leads to poor secondary sexual development and eunuchoid skeletal proportions.
  • SEXUAL INFANTILISM
  • Testes remain small, the penis fails to enlarge, the scrotum does not develop the marked rugae characteristic of puberty
  • Absent or very sparse axillary and pubic hair
  • Absent or very sparse facial, chest, upper abdominal and back hair
  • No erections
  • Inadequate spermatogenesis
  • SOMATIC CHANGES
  • Tall stature (or normal final height) with eunuchoid skeletal proportions (upper segment( crown to pubis) to lower segment( pubis to floor) ratio<1; similar because of the relatively greater growth in the upper extremities, the arm span of eunuchoid individuals exceeds height by 5 cm or more
  • Muscle mass does not develop fully, deposition of adipose tissue around the pelvic girdle
  • Low peak bone mass, Delayed bone age
  • High-pitched voice
  • Pale skin, and precocious appearance of wrinkles
  • Psychological disturbances
  • ↓ libidou

Clinical presentation #35

  • MH with postpubertal onset (testicular failure occurring after puberty)
  • Decreased libido, erectile dysfunction, and low energy.
  • Atrophy of the testes → small testes with a mushy or soft consistency
  • Atrophy of prostate
  • Spermatogenesis disturbances
  • Infertility
  • Normal ♂ hair distribution but reduced amount, sparse beard growth
  • Pale skin, fine wrinkles in the corners of the mouth and eyes
  • Central fat distribution, muscle hypotrophy
  • Gynecomastia
  • Osteoporosis
  • Anaemia (mild).
  • +/- hot flushes

Evaluation of Male Hypogonadism #36

HORMONAL ASSESSMENT: Gonadotropin and steroid measurement #37

  • Initial testing consists of measurement of total testosterone ( 7-10 a.m.) (at least 2 measurements)
  • LH, FSH- the primary use of basal FSH, LH concentrations is to distinguish between hypergonadotropic hypogonadism (primary gonadal failure) and hypogonadotropic hypogonadism (secondary gonadal failure)
  • → LH, FSH –low-normal/ ↓ + ↓ T (testosterone) = hypogonadotropic hypogonadism
  • → ↑ LH, FSH + ↓ T= hypergonadotropic hypogonadism( primary testicular disease)
  • SEMEN ANALYSIS
  • =the most important test in the evaluation of male infertility, the best means of assessing sperm production and function in the postpubertal male.
  • ! With some exceptions, a normal semen analysis excludes gonadal dysfunction
  • →masturbation after 2 to 7 days of sexual abstinence
  • Normal semen:
  • a volume of more than 2 to 4 mL,
  • with 10-20 x 106 or more sperms per milliliter.
  • more than 40 percent of the sperm ejaculated are motile (progressive and nonprogressive motility), more than 32 percent have progressive motility, and
  • ≥30% or more should have normal morphology/ more than 4 percent have normal morphology (using "strict" Tygerberg methods).

Additional testing to determine etiology #38

Slide 39 #39

  • If primary gonadal failure is identified  the peripheral leukocyte karyotype (e.g., to exclude Klinefelter’s syndrome, the most common sex chromosome anomaly)
  • + other genetic tests may include testing for Y-chromosome microdeletions.
  • In secondary gonadal failure (gonadotrophin deficiency): DO
  • pituitary MRI scan,
  • prolactin levels,
  • Fe, iron saturation and
  • other pituitary function tests are needed ( evaluate for other pituitary hormonal deficiencies by measurement of the serum concentrations of cortisol at 8 AM and of freeT4)
  • Dynamic test: h CG stimulation test→ widely used to quantitatively assess the ability of the testes to produce testosterone.
  • ►useful for examining Leydig function especially in prepubertal boys, to confirm the presence of testicular tissue in the evaluation of cryptorchidism (abdominal undescended testes)/anorchia
  • Human chorionic gonadotropin (h CG) – biologic actions similar to those of LH ( (+) the synthesis and secretion of testicular steroids in Leydig cells)
  • Do T before and 72 h and 96 h after a single im dose of hCG (5000ui in adults or 100UI/kg in children)
  • → a normal response: a doubling of the T level
  • → 0/↓ response= absence of functioning testicular tissue
  • → cryptorchidism: T will rise
  • → anorchia : no response

GnRH (other GnRH agonists) test: #40

  •  assess the functional integrity of the gonadotroph tissue.
  • It was/is sought to be useful in adolescents ♂ to distinguish delayed puberty from a more serious problem (hypogonadotropic hypogonadism)
  • → Do FSH, LH at 0’ and 30’ after adm. of 100ug of GnRH iv.
  • In normal men → LH ↑ 4-5 * basal levels while FSH ↑2* basal values
  • Patients with destructive lesion of the pituitary and those with long-standing hypogonadism due to hypothalamic disorders ( secondary hypogonadism): no response/ partial response
  • Scrotal US (testicular volume/blood flow with Doppler/presence of hydrocele, etc.).
  • TESTICULAR BIOPSY
  • →normal-sized testes and azoospermia in order to distinguish between spermatogenic failure and ductal obstruction
  • →For treatment of male infertility: testicular biopsies are also done to perform testicular sperm extraction for possible intracytoplasmic sperm injection (ICSI) into ova.

MH treatment #41

  • = replacement treatment
  • Treatment aims
  • • Induction of puberty and then maintenance of secondary sexual characteristics.
  • • Libido and sexual function improvement, (+mood and well-being, muscle mass and strength) and osteoporosis prevention in ♂ with testicular failure occurring after puberty.
  • DRUGS:
  • Intramuscularly:
  • TESTOSTERONE enanthate, cypionate or mixture of T esters :initiate with 50 mg im every 4 weeks → ↑ of 50 mg every 6–12 months → adult dose: 150-250mg every 2-4 weeks;
  • TESTOSTERONE UNDECANOAT (NEBIDO) 750–1000 mg every 10–14 weeks
  • Transdermal (TD)
  • A testosterone gel (AndroGel 1%; Testim 1%) that is applied daily to the abdomen, shoulders, or upper arms also results in physiologic concentrations of testosterone.
  • ! !! In hypogonadal boys : institute androgen therapy between the ages 12-13 years (since it may cause premature fusion of the epiphyses in an adolescent, which may result in some loss of potential height.)
  • Side effects: gynecomastia, erytrocytosis, sleep apnea Contraindications: prostatic carcinoma
  • !!! Androgen replacement therapy does not restore fertility
  • In patients with hypogonadism due to inadequate gonadotropin secretion, spermatogenesis (and virilization) may be induced by exogenous gonadotropin injections (hCG, FSH)

Klinefelter syndrome (XXY seminiferous dysgenesis) #42

  • =the most common genetic cause of male hypogonadism, occurring in one of 600 male births.
  • The underlying defect is the presence of an extra X Cz, the usual chromosomal karyotype being either 47XXY (classic form) or 46, XY/47, XXY (mosaic form) Clinical manifestations will depend on the age of diagnosis. Patients with mosaicism tend to have less severe clinical features.
  • Pathophysiology
  • The XXY genotype is usually due to maternal meiotic nondisjunction → an egg with two X Cs ( ! The frequency of meiotic errors correlates positively with maternal age)
  • Histologic changes in the testes: hyalinization and fibrosis of the tubules, absence of spermatogenesis (← obliteration of the seminiferous tubules)
  • Leydig cells are also abnormal

CLINICAL FEATURES #43

  • → related to the degree of ↓ T production and sometimes to alterations in the androgen receptor
  • ► ↑ Tall stature (↑leg length); abnormal skeletal proportions that are not truly eunuchoid (pubis-to-floor height is greater than crown-to-pubis height, but arm span is less than total height).
  • Is not secondary to androgen deficiency but is probably related to the underlying chromosomal abnormality
  • ►Small (<2 cm in longest axis, and 4ml in volume), firm testes
  • ► Manifestations of androgen deficiency:
  • Penis and scrotum undergo varying degrees of development during puberty, with some individuals appearing normal!
  • Gynecomastia (50%)
  • ↓libidou and erectile dysfunction
  • ↓facial hair, axillary hair, infertility
  • Osteoporosis
  • ►↑ prevalence of cognitive impairment ( patients with three or more X chromosomes uniformly have severe cognitive impairment)
  • ► Learning disabilities and poor impulse control, feeling of inadequacy, dissocial behavior
  • Patients with sex chromosome mosaicism (XY/47XXY) typically manifest a mild phenotype

Klinefelter syndrome #44

  • LABORATORY FINDINGS
  • Chromosomal analysis (Karyotyping)→ 47, XXY karyotype in 80%→ definitive diagnosis
  • T↓, ↑FSH (especially) ,↑LH, FSH>LH
  • Semen analysis: Azoospermia (some with mosaic Klinefelter syndrome have variable degree of oligozoospermia)
  • The buccal smear is chromatin-positive (>20% of cells having a Barr body)
  • TREATMENT
  • → directed toward androgen replacement therapy
  • → reduction mamoplasty if gynecomastia= significant cosmetic problem
  • →For those desiring fertility, sperm may be extracted directly from the testes in about half of the patients and used for ICSI with a live birth rate of up to 20%.
  • However, couples should be counselled about the ↑ risk of chromosomal abnormalities in offspring.
